summary: Tenofovir alafenamide is a prodrug of tenofovir used for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in adults and adolescents with compensated liver disease, and (in fixed-dose combinations such as Biktarvy and Descovy) for HIV-1. Compared with tenofovir disoproxil, it delivers tenofovir more efficiently into hepatocytes and lymphoid cells, achieving antiviral activity at a much lower dose with lower circulating tenofovir levels and improved renal and bone safety. It carries a BOXED WARNING that discontinuing anti-HBV therapy can cause severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B, and (for HIV-active products) that it must not be used as monotherapy in patients who are or may be co-infected with HIV.

moa: Tenofovir alafenamide is a phosphonamidate prodrug of tenofovir (2'-deoxyadenosine monophosphate analog). It is more stable in plasma than tenofovir disoproxil and is taken up efficiently into hepatocytes and lymphoid cells, where it is hydrolyzed to tenofovir and then phosphorylated by cellular kinases to the active metabolite tenofovir diphosphate. Tenofovir diphosphate inhibits viral replication by competing with the natural substrate deoxyadenosine triphosphate and, after incorporation into the growing viral DNA by HBV reverse transcriptase/polymerase (or HIV-1 reverse transcriptase), causes DNA chain termination. The higher intracellular delivery allows efficacy at a lower dose with lower systemic tenofovir exposure, reducing renal and bone toxicity relative to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate.

Co-administration with products that are contraindicated with the specific combination regimen (for HIV combination products)

Decompensated (Child-Pugh B/C) cirrhosis - not recommended for HBV
Severe renal impairment off dialysis (CrCl <15 mL/min)

Concurrent use with potent P-gp inducers (reduce efficacy)

preg: There are insufficient human data to establish drug-associated risk; animal studies at clinically relevant exposures did not show adverse developmental effects. The decision to use in pregnancy should weigh the benefit of maternal HBV/HIV control against potential risk, ideally in consultation with a specialist and an antiretroviral pregnancy registry where applicable.
lact: For chronic hepatitis B, the decision to breastfeed should consider the unknown infant exposure and maternal need; tenofovir is excreted in human milk in low amounts. For HIV, mothers in the US and similar settings should be advised not to breastfeed because of the risk of HIV transmission. Follow local guidelines and product-specific advice.
renal: No dose adjustment is needed for the 25 mg dose in patients with estimated CrCl >=15 mL/min, or in patients with CrCl <15 mL/min who are receiving chronic hemodialysis (give after dialysis on dialysis days). It is not recommended in patients with CrCl <15 mL/min who are not on hemodialysis. Renal impairment, including acute renal failure and Fanconi syndrome, has been reported with tenofovir prodrugs; assess renal parameters before and during therapy.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is required in mild to moderate hepatic impairment. It has not been studied in patients with decompensated (Child-Pugh B or C) hepatic impairment and is not recommended in this setting. Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B have occurred after discontinuation (boxed warning) - monitor liver function for at least several months after stopping.

major: P-glycoprotein inducers (rifampin, rifabutin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, oxcarbazepine, St. John's wort) - decrease tenofovir alafenamide concentrations and may reduce efficacy; co-administration not recommended
For HIV combination products: numerous regimen-specific contraindicated drugs - consult the specific product label
moderate: Drugs that affect P-gp/BCRP (certain inhibitors) - may increase tenofovir alafenamide exposure
Other nephrotoxic agents - additive renal risk; monitor renal function
minor: Antacids/H2 blockers/PPIs may affect absorption of some combination components - check specific product
interactions.food: Should be taken with food, which increases tenofovir alafenamide exposure.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid or limit alcohol; it is hepatotoxic and can worsen underlying liver disease in HBV patients.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause changes in serum creatinine and urine markers; monitor renal parameters and liver enzymes.

serious: Severe acute exacerbation of hepatitis B after discontinuation (boxed)
Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis (class effect)
New onset or worsening renal impairment / Fanconi syndrome
emergency: Severe hepatitis B flare with hepatic decompensation after stopping therapy
Lactic acidosis (rapid breathing, weakness, muscle pain)

monitoring: HBV DNA and HBV serology (HBeAg/HBsAg) for response
Liver function tests during therapy and for several months after discontinuation
HIV status before and during treatment
Serum creatinine, estimated CrCl, urine glucose and protein
Bone mineral density in patients at risk of osteoporosis/fracture
counsel: Take one tablet once a day with food and do not stop without talking to your doctor
Stopping suddenly can cause your hepatitis B to flare badly - your liver will be monitored for months if you stop
Get tested for HIV before starting; this medicine alone is not enough to treat HIV
Report yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine, severe tiredness, muscle pain, or fast breathing
Avoid alcohol and tell your doctor about all other medicines, including herbal products like St. John's wort
Keep all appointments for blood tests of your liver and kidney function
pk: Antiviral suppression of HBV DNA over days to weeks
Plasma Tmax ~0.5-1 hour (tenofovir alafenamide); higher intracellular levels
Plasma ~0.5 hour (alafenamide); intracellular tenofovir diphosphate ~150-180 hours
Once-daily dosing maintains suppression; long intracellular persistence
Store at room temperature; keep in original container, protect from moisture
pearls: BOXED WARNING: stopping anti-HBV therapy can cause severe acute hepatitis B exacerbation - monitor LFTs for months after discontinuation
Always test for HIV first; do not use as HBV monotherapy in HIV co-infection (resistance risk) - relevant for HIV-active combinations
Lower dose and lower plasma tenofovir than tenofovir disoproxil = better renal and bone safety profile
Avoid potent P-gp inducers (rifampin, St. John's wort, some anticonvulsants) which reduce efficacy
Take with food to maximize absorption
Not recommended in decompensated cirrhosis or CrCl <15 mL/min off dialysis
missed: If you miss a dose and remember within about 18 hours of the usual time, take it with food as soon as possible, then take the next dose at the regular time. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose - do not take two doses at once. Never stop the drug on your own.
overdose: There is limited experience with overdose. Monitor for evidence of toxicity and provide standard supportive treatment, including observation of clinical status and vital signs. Tenofovir is efficiently removed by hemodialysis (about 54% of the dose), which may be used if needed.
